content: For the purpose of this report, only data from healthcare workers were analyzed. A total of 190 individuals responded to the survey, of which 178 (94%) identified as healthcare workers. Among these healthcare workers, 61% (n = 108) were male, and the majority of respondents were aged between 45 and 54 years (n = 46, 26%). Of the 178 healthcare workers, 55% (n = 97) were specialists, including hepatologists (n = 60, 33%), infectious disease physicians (n = 23, 13%), and gastroenterologists (n = 14, 8%). Additionally, 16% (n = 28) of respondents were scientists with expertise in hepatitis B diagnosis and therapy. Perceived Priorities for Hepatitis B Elimination The highest priorities identified for achieving hepatitis B elimination were increasing HBV screening and diagnosis (80% of respondents) and optimizing strategies to prevent mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) (79% of respondents). These were followed by increasing access to antiviral therapy. Regional Distribution of Respondents Most respondents reported working in sub-Saharan Africa (37%), followed by South and South-East Asia (22%) and Europe (16%). Availability of HBV Diagnostic Testing Respondents were asked about the availability of diagnostic assays in their settings. HBsAg ELISA testing was available in 75% (n = 133/178) of settings, while HBsAg rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) were available in 77% (n = 138/178). Molecular testing for HBV DNA using PCR was also reported to be available in 77% (n = 137) of settings. However, sub-Saharan Africa reported the lowest availability of both serological and molecular HBV testing. A significant proportion of respondents (82%, n = 139) strongly agreed or agreed that a point-of-care test for HBeAg would add value to hepatitis B care in their locations. HDV Diagnostics and Testing Only 20% of respondents reported routine screening for anti-HDV among HBsAg-positive individuals in their practice. This rate was even lower in sub-Saharan Africa (3%) and South and South-East Asia (12%). HDV RNA PCR testing was least available in sub-Saharan Africa (13%), South and South-East Asia (20%), and South America (30%). The remaining 22% (n = 39) stated that children under 18 years were not offered antiviral therapy in their settings. Treatment Prioritization Respondents were asked about their agreement with treatment scenarios. The highest level of agreement (78%) was for prioritizing treatment for individuals with chronic hepatitis B and advanced hepatic fibrosis (stage 3 or 4). Other scenarios, such as treating patients with elevated ALT levels or those over 40 years of age regardless of HBV DNA, HBeAg, or ALT status, received varying levels of agreement. WHO Guidelines Update The World Health Organization (WHO) is in the process of updating its guidelines on the prevention, care, and treatment of chronic hepatitis B. This includes expanded criteria for treatment eligibility, use of non-invasive tests, and lowering thresholds for diagnosing cirrhosis and fibrosis. The updated guidelines will also address the use of antivirals for preventing mother-to-child transmission, simplified service delivery, and treatment for children and adolescents. Survey on Healthcare Workers’ Preferences A survey was conducted to gather healthcare workers' perspectives on treating children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis B. A total of 150 individuals from 41 countries responded. Most respondents were pediatricians (70%) based in tertiary centers (80%). The most commonly used drugs for treating children and adolescents with hepatitis B over the past five years were tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir, and lamivudine. These drugs were also the most commonly registered and licensed in respondents’ countries and were often provided through national insurance or government-funded programs. Criteria for Treatment Most respondents prioritized treating children and adolescents with elevated ALT levels or those who were immunosuppressed. Other factors influencing treatment decisions included HBeAg status, ALT levels, viral load, and evidence of liver fibrosis. Only a small number of respondents supported treating all children and adolescents with hepatitis B. Treatment for Adolescents vs. Children Half of the respondents believed that treatment criteria for adolescents should be the same as for adults. However, 69% suggested that treatment criteria for children aged 0–11 years should differ from those for adults. The main reasons cited were the immune-tolerant phase and normal ALT levels in children, absence of fibrosis and cirrhosis, and lower risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Concerns about treatment adherence, dosing for children, and potential toxicity and side effects, particularly on growth, were also highlighted. Preferences for Antiviral Regimens Most respondents (69%) agreed that the choice of antiviral therapy for adolescents should be the same as for adults. However, only 17% believed that treatments for children should be the same as for adults. Safety concerns, growth and development considerations, and the need for child-specific formulations were the main reasons for preferring different regimens for children. Conclusion This survey provided valuable insights from a diverse group of healthcare workers worldwide regarding their priorities and preferences for treating children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis B. These findings will contribute to the development of updated WHO guidelines on hepatitis B care and treatment.
